sections.title_en: The Meaning of the Priesthood in Israel
sections.body_en:
The kohanim had two main roles: one, to educate and to teach halakha in Israel, as it is said (Malakhi 2:7): "For the lips of the kohen shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek Torah from his mouth." The second, to increase kindness and peace in Israel, just as Aharon the kohen was "one who loves peace and pursues peace, who loves people and brings them near to the Torah" (Avot 1:12). It is related of Aharon the kohen that he knew how to make peace between a person and his fellow and between a man and his wife, and several thousands in Israel were called Aharon after him, for were it not for Aharon they would not have come into the world: he would make peace between a man and his wife, and through this they came together again, and they would call the name of the child born 'Aharon' (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 12). These two roles drew their inspiration from the service of the kohanim in the Temple on behalf of all Israel.

In order to enable the kohanim to develop these two foundations, wisdom and kindness, the Torah determined that the kohanim would not receive an inheritance in the Land of Israel, and their livelihood would be from the terumot and priestly gifts that the children of Israel would grant them, and through this the kohanim could free themselves for Torah study and for educating and guiding the public. And by receiving their gifts from the Israelites, they would be bound to them with love and respect, and would take pains to fulfil their spiritual mission for the sake of all Israel. Likewise, since they had no lands and did not take part in economic competition, they could more easily develop within themselves love and kindness towards the whole people.

Love is the foundation of Birkat Kohanim (the Priestly Blessing), for out of the love of the kohanim for the people of Israel they are worthy to be the agents who bless Israel in the name of God. And this is the wording of the blessing: "who has sanctified us with the holiness of Aharon and commanded us to bless His people Israel with love."

The poskim wrote that any kohen whom the congregation hates, or who hates the congregation, or even hates one person, may not recite Birkat Kohanim. And if he blesses out of hatred, he brings danger upon himself. Therefore, either he should completely erase the hatred from his heart, or he should leave the synagogue before Birkat Kohanim, for its essence is to bless Israel with love (MB 128:37; Rav Tzvi Yehuda, Olat Re'iya 2, 413).

Originally all the firstborn sons were meant to be kohanim, so that the whole public with all its families would be connected personally and as families to the men of the priesthood, something that would certainly have contributed to the general spiritual level of the people. But after the firstborn sons took part together with the rest of the people in the sin of the golden calf, they fell from their level, and in their place the tribe of Levi, which had not taken part in the sin, was sanctified, and from it the members of the family of Aharon were chosen to be kohanim.

Apparently, the idea of the firstborn is indeed an ideal idea. Through the priesthood of the firstborn, all the families would have been connected to holiness, for in every family there would have been a kohen wholly engaged in matters of holiness. And it is not a matter of just any representative, but of the firstborn, who is the most honoured of the sons, and so his sacred destiny too would have gained an important status. But in practice we did not succeed in realising this wonderful idea, and instead of the firstborn influencing the people as a whole, the general mundane atmosphere blurred the distinctiveness of the firstborn, and they were drawn after the people and sinned. In order to educate kohanim who would truly be men of spirit, not influenced by the noisy mundane life, it was necessary to dedicate a whole family to the role of the priesthood, a family whose whole role would be to strengthen holiness and spirituality in Israel. Therefore, after the firstborn sinned, Aharon and his sons were chosen to be kohanim. It is worth noting here that some say that in the future to come the firstborn will return to their level and, together with the kohanim, serve in the priesthood (Tikkunim Ḥadashim of the Ramḥal, end of 54; Or Ha-ḥayim, Bamidbar 3:45; Pinkesei Ha-Re'iya, Pinkas 1 (Boisk), 6).

sections.title_en: Kohanim and Levites Who Supported the Fighting
sections.body_en:
The kohanim had a further important role: to strengthen the fighters when they went out to war in defence of the people and the Land. For this purpose, in addition to the kohen gadol, who was responsible for the service of the Temple, they anointed with the anointing oil another kohen, called the 'kohen anointed for war' (kohen meshuaḥ milḥama), whose role was to encourage the fighters of Israel with words of faith, and to say to them before the war: "Hear, O Israel, you are drawing near today to battle against your enemies; let your heart not be faint, do not fear, and do not be alarmed, and do not be terrified of them. For the Lord your God is He who goes with you, to fight for you against your enemies, to save you" (Devarim 20:2-4).

Likewise the kohanim are commanded to blow trumpets in order to encourage the fighters to courage and trust in God, as it is said (Bamidbar 10:8-9): "And the sons of Aharon, the kohanim, shall blow the trumpets, and they shall be to you an everlasting statute throughout your generations. And when you go to war in your land against the adversary who oppresses you, you shall sound an alarm with the trumpets, and you shall be remembered before the Lord your God, and you shall be saved from your enemies." And so they did in the war against Midyan, as it is said (ibid. 31:6): "And Moshe sent them, a thousand of each tribe, to the army, them and Pinḥas son of Elazar the kohen, to the army, with the holy vessels and the trumpets for the alarm in his hand." Likewise in the war of Yeriḥo, the kohanim had an important role in leading the war from the spiritual aspect, as it is said (Yehoshua 6:4): "And seven kohanim shall carry seven shofarot of rams' horns before the ark, and on the seventh day you shall go around the city seven times, and the kohanim shall blow the shofarot." And likewise in the war of Aviya king of Yehuda (II Divrei Ha-yamim 13:12-14).

In addition, during the fighting the kohanim would carry the ark and accompany Israel in their wars, and through this the Shekhina rested in the camp of Israel and they merited help from Heaven, as it is said (Bamidbar 10:35): "And it was, when the ark set out, that Moshe said: Rise up, O Lord, and let Your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate You flee before You." And likewise it is said (Devarim 23:15): "For the Lord your God walks in the midst of your camp, to save you and to give up your enemies before you", and they explained that this refers to the ark of the Lord that was in the midst of the camp (Pesikta Zutarta, Yere'im and others). And likewise it is said (Bamidbar 14:44-45) of the ma'apilim, who went up to fight without the consent of Moshe our teacher and without the accompaniment of the ark, and were defeated: "But they presumed to go up to the top of the mountain, but the ark of the covenant of the Lord and Moshe did not depart from the midst of the camp. And the Amalekite and the Canaanite who dwelt in that mountain came down, and struck them and beat them down as far as Ḥorma." And likewise, when they needed to inquire of the Urim and Tummim on matters of the war, they would inquire before the ark (Shoftim 20:27; I Shmuel 14:18). And in the ark was "the Name and all its epithets" (Sota 43a, and they disagree as to which ark is meant). Presumably the kohanim who carried the ark were fierce fighters, in order to protect the ark, for the enemy would make great efforts to capture it and thereby decide the battle, like the capture of the flag in many wars. And since they were fierce fighters, in a difficult hour they stood in the breach against rebels and enemies, just as the Ḥashmona'im led the revolt against the Greeks who decreed to make Israel abandon their religion.1

The Levites had a further important role, to be police officers (shotrim), as it is said (II Divrei Ha-yamim 19:11): "And the Levites shall be officers before you; be strong and act, and may the Lord be with the good" (Yevamot 86b). As part of this role they were apparently responsible for granting exemption to soldiers from a discretionary war, and for guarding the soldiers so that they would not be afraid and flee, as it is said (Devarim 20:5-9): "And the officers shall speak to the people, saying: What man is there who has built a new house and has not dedicated it? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man dedicate it. And what man is there who has planted a vineyard and has not redeemed its fruit? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man redeem it. And what man is there who has betrothed a woman and has not taken her? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man take her. And the officers shall speak further to the people and say: What man is there who is fearful and faint-hearted? Let him go and return to his house, lest his brothers' heart melt like his heart. And it shall be, when the officers have finished speaking to the people, that they shall appoint captains of the armies at the head of the people."

And since a significant part of the roles of the Levites was to serve as police officers in Israel, it seems that after the war began, they were responsible for strengthening the fighters and punishing those who fled from the battle, and as the Sages said (Mishna Sota 8:6), they would station sentries behind the fighters, that is, mighty officers, to raise up those who fell in the war. And further sentries behind them, "with iron axes in their hands, and whoever wishes to turn back, they have the authority to cut his legs, for the beginning of flight is defeat…".2

notes_en.en:
At the same time as the fighters went out to battle, the Levites would sing and pray for the vanguard of the fighting army, as it is said in the days of Yehoshafat: "And the Levites, of the children of the Kehatites and of the children of the Korḥites, stood up to praise the Lord, God of Israel, with an exceedingly loud voice… And when they began to sing and to praise, the Lord set ambushes against the children of Ammon, Moav and Mount Se'ir, who had come against Yehuda, and they were struck down" (II Divrei Ha-yamim 20:19-22). And some say that the psalm 'The Lord answer you in the day of trouble' in Tehillim (chapter 20) was written for the Levites praying for the fighters in battle (Meiri, Sota 42b).
As we learned above, the kohanim went out with the ark to accompany the fighters of Israel in their war, and the ark was the expression of God being in the midst of the camp of Israel. And likewise in the days of David, the ark was with the fighters in the siege of Rabbat Benei Ammon (II Shmuel 11:11). The question is with which ark they went out. It is said in Devarim (10:1-2) that God commanded Moshe to build an ark in which he would place the second tablets. According to Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish in the Tosefta (Sota 7:17-18), and in the Yerushalmi (Shekalim 6:1; Sota 8:3), in this ark there were at first the fragments of the tablets together with the second tablets. After Betzalel built the ark of the covenant, the second tablets were transferred to it, and the fragments of the tablets remained in Moshe's ark, and with it they would go out to wars – except when the sons of Eli took out the ark of the covenant to the war against the Philistines, and they were punished in that the ark was captured (I Shmuel 4–6). And so wrote Rashi (Devarim 10:1), Rabbeinu Baḥya (there), the Ri (Tosafot, Eruvin 63b) and others. And the Tosafot Ha-Rosh wrote (Sota 42a) that after Shlomo built the Temple, the fragments of the tablets too were transferred to the ark of the covenant, and in Moshe's ark there remained the Name of God and its epithets. On the other hand, according to the Sages in the Yerushalmi there were not two arks but only the ark of the covenant, and it is the ark that Moshe made (Ibn Ezra, Devarim 10:1), or after Betzalel built the ark of the covenant, Moshe's ark was hidden away (Ramban there). However, even according to this opinion, Abarbanel explained (Bamidbar 10:11) that there was another ark besides the ark of the covenant, in which they placed the ephod and the breastplate with the Urim and Tummim, which contained the Names of God, and with it they would go out to war.

Mishna Sota 8:6: "'And it shall be, when the officers have finished speaking to the people, that they shall appoint captains of the armies at the head of the people' – and at the rear of the people (behind the fighters) they station sentries (mighty men) before them (to raise up those who fall), and others behind them (who were to punish those who fled) with iron axes in their hands, and whoever wishes to turn back, they have the authority to cut his legs, for the beginning of flight is defeat…" And since this too is a police role, like a military police, there is room to say that the Levites filled this role.
Regarding the role of the Levites as police officers it is said: "And David was old and full of days, and he made Shlomo his son king over Israel… And the Levites were counted from the age of thirty years and upward… and officers and judges, six thousand" (I Divrei Ha-yamim 23:1-4). And likewise it is said: "Of the Yitzharites, Kenanyahu and his sons were for the outward business over Israel, as officers and judges" (ibid. 26:29). And likewise in the days of Yehoshafat: "And the Levites shall be officers before you; be strong and act, and may the Lord be with the good" (ibid. II 19:11). And likewise in the days of Yoshiyahu: "And they were over the bearers of burdens, and directed all who did the work in every manner of service; and of the Levites there were scribes and officers and gatekeepers" (ibid. 34:13). And likewise they said (Yevamot 86b): "At first [in the days of the First Temple] they would appoint officers only from the Levites, as it is said: And the Levites shall be officers before you. Now they appoint officers only from Israelites" (because only a few of them came up for the building of the Second Temple). And likewise the Sages said (Sifrei Devarim 15) that the Levites were the officers who accompanied the judges to punish the sinners. And Rabbi David Pardo explained that this role belongs to the Levites because their root is in the attribute of gevura (might) (Sifrei de-Vei Rav, Devarim 1:15), and in this they continued their role from Egypt and from stopping and punishing the sinners at the sin of the calf (Meshekh Ḥokhma, Bamidbar 9:9-10; Malbim, Shemot 32:27). And likewise we find in Rashi (Bamidbar 26:13): "And I found in the Jerusalem Talmud (cited in other midrashim) that when Aharon died and the clouds of glory departed, and the Canaanites came to fight against Israel, and they resolved to return to Egypt, and they went back eight stages from Hor Ha-har to Mosera… the sons of Levi pursued them to bring them back, and killed seven families of them, and of the sons of Levi four families fell…" And so wrote Rav Goren (Torat Ha-medina, p. 238).
However, the implication is that they appointed judges and officers from each and every tribe (Devarim 16:18); and one may say that the meaning is that they appointed from the sons of Levi who lived in the inheritance of that tribe. And some explain that in addition to the officers from the members of the tribe, the Levites too were officers, with judicial powers (Be'er Sheva, Sota 42a; Aseh Lekha Rav 3:48).

sections.body_en:
The Torah designated special mitzvot for the kohanim in order to sanctify them and prepare them for their spiritual role. In general one may say that the prohibitions special to the kohanim are intended to elevate them above the complicated and difficult sides of reality. In two areas the Torah restricted the kohanim: in the area of the family and in the area of purity.

In the area of the family: a kohen may not marry a divorcee, a zona or a ḥalala, as it is said (Vayikra 21:7): "They shall not take a woman who is a zona or a ḥalala, nor shall they take a woman divorced from her husband, for he is holy to his God." The prohibition of a divorcee includes also a ḥalutza, but a kohen may marry a widow. The prohibition of marrying a zona applies to a woman who had relations with a man whom, according to the Torah, she is forbidden to marry, such as a gentile, or her father or brother or one of her other relatives forbidden to her. Likewise a married woman who committed adultery, even if afterwards she was widowed, is forbidden to a kohen. And although generally a zona is the term for one who gives herself over for payment, and some also call so a woman who had relations outside the framework of marriage, for the purpose of this halakha a zona is considered only one who had relations with a man whom by Torah law she is forbidden to marry; but one who had relations with a stranger without marriage, even if she did so for payment, since in principle she could have married him, is not called a zona for the purpose of this halakha, and she may still marry a kohen. A kohen may also not marry a convert (SA EH 6:8). The ḥalala forbidden to a kohen is a daughter whose father profaned his priesthood in begetting her, such as a daughter born to a kohen and a divorcee; however, to an Israelite she is permitted.

The second area is purity, according to which kohanim may not become impure through a dead person – that is, they may not touch a dead person or be with him in one room or under one roof. Only for one of his first-degree relatives may a kohen become impure, that is, be with him under one roof, and in a time of need even touch him. The first-degree relatives are: his father, his mother, his brother, his unmarried sister, his son, his daughter, and of course his wife. As it is said (Vayikra 21:1): "And the Lord said to Moshe: Speak to the kohanim, the sons of Aharon, and say to them: none shall become impure for a dead person among his people, except for his relative who is near to him, for his mother and for his father, and for his son and for his daughter and for his brother; and for his virgin sister who is near to him, who has had no husband – for her he may become impure." Likewise, if it happened that a kohen met on his way, outside a settlement, a 'met mitzva', that is, an abandoned dead person, whose place no one knows of and whom no one is caring for to bury, the kohen is commanded to do kindness with the dead person and bury him, even though he is not his relative, and in the process he will need to touch him and become impure.

Rav Kook explained that according to the absolute concepts of eternity, death is a false vision. In truth the soul passes from world to world, from a lower world to a higher world, and only in this world does death appear as something terrible and shocking. And since the role of the kohanim is to express the ideas of eternity, which emphasise life and kindness, the Torah distanced them from death, so that emotionally they would not be so influenced by the sorrow and despair that accompany it (Orot Ha-kodesh 2, p. 380). However, this distancing is not absolute, and for their relatives or for a met mitzva they become impure; but nevertheless the Torah distanced them relatively from death.

However, for the kohen gadol, who stands at the head of the kohanim, the Torah established stricter laws. For because of the exalted level of his role, he must be more connected to the eternal world, and keep further away from the difficult and complicated sides of life. Therefore, the kohen gadol may not become impure even for his relatives, and only for a met mitzva may he become impure. Likewise the kohen gadol may not marry a widow, and the kohen gadol could marry only a virgin. As it is said (Vayikra 21:10): "And the kohen who is greatest among his brothers, upon whose head the anointing oil was poured, and who is consecrated to wear the garments, shall not let the hair of his head grow loose, nor rend his garments (in mourning for his relatives). Nor shall he go in to any dead body, nor become impure for his father or for his mother. Nor shall he go out of the Sanctuary, nor profane the Sanctuary of his God, for the crown of the anointing oil of his God is upon him; I am the Lord. And he shall take a wife in her virginity. A widow, or a divorcee, or a ḥalala, or a zona – these he shall not take; but a virgin of his own people shall he take as a wife, and he shall not profane his seed among his people, for I am the Lord who sanctifies him."

It is worth knowing that the Temple was intended to serve as a pattern from which we learn how to establish the values of holiness in the life of all Israel and of the world: the Holy of Holies corresponds to faith, the special quality of Israel, the Torah and the covenant of marriage. The table in the Sanctuary corresponds to all the kinds of work and livelihoods; the menora in the Sanctuary corresponds to all the sciences and crafts; the inner altar corresponds to prayer; the outer altar corresponds to sacrifice and self-dedication. Similarly, one should learn from the service of the kohanim in the Temple regarding all the kinds of work that help the settlement and improvement of the world. Just as the kohanim must sanctify themselves for the service of the Temple and beware of things that might distract their minds from their service, so every person must find a moral value in his work, and like a kohen purify and sanctify himself for it. For example, if he is a teacher or a doctor, he should see to it that he sleeps well, so that he can fulfil his role properly. If he is an engineer, he should not rest on his laurels, but expand his knowledge and focus his mind so that he can fulfil his role responsibly and add goodness and blessing in his work. And so in all kinds of work.

And there are exceptional individuals who are like kohanim gedolim, such as a doctor with rare abilities to save life, who must sanctify himself like a kohen gadol entering the Holy of Holies, and not go out from the sanctuary of his work, even for the sake of his relatives. And even if, in the middle of his son's wedding canopy, he is suddenly summoned to the hospital, he should hastily take leave of his son, his wife and his guests, and they will know where he is going and will accompany him with prayer that he succeed in fulfilling his mission, to save the patient who is now struggling between life and death. And likewise a commander in an elite unit, who must always be ready for every call: if, while he is accompanying his wife to the birth of their son, he is suddenly called to the aid of Israel against an adversary, he should take leave of her in peace; and just as all Israel would pray on Yom Kippur for the kohen gadol that he come out of the Holy of Holies in peace, so his wife will pray for him at the time of her giving birth that he return from battle in peace to see their son.

Having learned that the sons of Aharon, the kohanim, were chosen to bless Israel because their role is to be the men of spirit and kindness among the people, there is room to ask: how is it possible that kohanim who are not righteous also bless Israel, since they have no merits for whose sake Israel should be blessed? Not only that, but even a kohen who commits transgressions, such as eating carrion and forbidden relations, is commanded to go up to the dukhan and fulfil the mitzva that God commanded the kohanim, to bless His people Israel with love.

The explanation of this is that in truth it is God who blesses His people Israel with love, and in order that the blessing be revealed in the world, we must express it with our lips, that is, we must do something that expresses our recognition that God is the source of blessing in the world. The kohanim as a whole are the group with the sacred role among the people of Israel, and therefore they are the ones who were commanded to be the agents who express the divine will to bless the people of Israel. But the blessing does not depend on the private righteousness of the kohen who blesses, but on the divine will to bless the people of Israel (Rambam, Hilkhot Tefilla 15:7; and see Olat Re'iya p. 283).

Therefore, even a wicked kohen who has sinned with many transgressions is commanded to recite Birkat Kohanim, because the blessing is from the Holy One, blessed be He, and not from the kohen. And if he refrains from blessing, he will only add another sin to his sins. And as the Rambam wrote on this in Hilkhot Tefilla (15:6): "One does not say to a wicked person: add (more) wickedness and refrain from the mitzvot."

However, regarding giving terumot and ma'asrot to the kohanim and Levites, it is a mitzva to give them to kohanim and Levites who are Torah scholars, who study and teach Torah. And as King Ḥizkiyahu instructed (II Divrei Ha-yamim 31:4): "And he told the people, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, to give the portion of the kohanim and the Levites, so that they might be strengthened in the Torah of the Lord." And only if there were no kohanim and Levites there who engage in Torah should one give the terumot and the tithe to kohanim and Levites who are not Torah scholars, because the whole tribe is designated for this, since it has no inheritance in the Land. However, as soon as kohanim and Levites who are Torah scholars arrive there, one should return to giving them the gifts (see Peninei Halakha, Kashrut 7:3, 1).

sections.title_en: The Transgressions That Disqualify a Kohen From Raising His Hands
sections.body_en:
However, there are sins that harm the holiness of the priesthood, such as a kohen who marries a divorcee or is not careful about becoming impure through the dead; and since the kohen sinned in prohibitions intended to protect his special holiness, the Sages penalised him that he not go up to the dukhan, and that he not be called up to the Torah for the first aliya designated for kohanim. And if he wishes to repent, he must first divorce his disqualified wife, and take a vow on the understanding of the public that he will no longer marry women forbidden to him, and after that he can again raise his hands and be called up to the Torah for the kohen's aliya. And likewise, if he was accustomed to become impure through the dead, he must accept upon himself that he will not again become impure through the dead (SA OḤ 128:40-41).

A kohen who worshipped idols is disqualified from reciting Birkat Kohanim. And we learn this from the law of the Temple service: just as a kohen who worshipped idols is disqualified from the Temple service, so he is disqualified from raising his hands (Menaḥot 109a, and Tosafot there). But if he has repented completely, he can again raise his hands (SA OḤ 128:37).

There are poskim who equate the law of one who desecrates Shabbat publicly, that is, before ten Jews, with the law of an idol worshipper, who may not go up to the dukhan (MB 128:134). But in practice the opinion of most poskim is that if he does not intend to provoke and rebel against the mitzvot of the Torah, even though he desecrates Shabbat, he may go up to the dukhan (see Peninei Halakha, Tefilla 20:10; Kashrut 29:13).

A kohen who has killed a person should not raise his hands, as it is said (Yeshayahu 1:15): "And when you spread forth your hands, I will hide My eyes from you… your hands are full of blood" (Berakhot 32b). That is, only hands that are clean of blood are fit for Birkat Kohanim. And just as it is forbidden to prepare stones for the altar with iron, because iron shortens a person's days, whereas the altar is meant to make peace and lengthen a person's days, so a kohen whose hands are stained with blood cannot raise his hands and bestow blessing and peace upon the people of Israel. The role of the kohen is to add kindness and life, like Aharon the kohen, who loved peace and pursued peace, and a kohen who has killed has damaged the foundation of his priesthood. And this is on condition that he killed not according to law; but a kohen who killed enemies of Israel in war is fit for Birkat Kohanim, in the manner of Pinḥas son of Elazar and the Ḥashmona'im, who fought the enemies of Israel and thereby expressed their priesthood.

Some say that repentance does not help a kohen who has killed a person (SA OḤ 128:35), and some say that it helps (Rema). And some say that for one who killed unintentionally repentance will help, and for one who killed deliberately repentance will not help.

In practice, a kohen who killed unintentionally must ask his rabbi to guide him in the order of his repentance, and to instruct him whether afterwards he can raise his hands. A kohen who unintentionally ran a person over and killed him is also disqualified from going up to the dukhan for Birkat Kohanim. However, if there was no negligence in his driving, according to all opinions, if he repents according to the instruction of a Torah scholar, he can afterwards again raise his hands (see Peninei Halakha, Tefilla 20:11).

sections.title_en: The Mitzva to Honour a Kohen
sections.body_en:
It is said in the Torah, in the passage of the kohanim (Vayikra 21:8): "And you shall sanctify him, for he offers the bread of your God; he shall be holy to you, for I the Lord who sanctifies you am holy." From here the Sages learned that one should honour the kohen and give him precedence in every matter of holiness. He recites the blessing first, and opens the speaking first, and even at a meal one should give the kohen precedence and give him a fine portion first.

Although the kohanim as a whole were chosen to be the men of wisdom and kindness among the people of Israel, this does not deny any other Jew the possibility of being a Torah scholar and a man of spirit. The meaning of the choice of the kohanim is to designate a whole family for matters of holiness, so that through this it will be easier for them to study and to advance, since all the members of the family engage in the same subjects and strengthen one another (above halakha 1). But it is clear that all Israel belong to matters of the spirit and of holiness, and so the Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Shemita Ve-yovel 13:13): "And not the tribe of Levi alone, but every single person of all who come into the world whose spirit moves him and whose understanding gives him insight to separate himself to stand before the Lord, to serve Him and to worship Him in order to know the Lord, and he walks uprightly as God made him, and he has removed from his neck the yoke of the many calculations that people have sought – this person has been sanctified as holy of holies, and the Lord will be his portion and his inheritance for ever and ever…"

And so is the halakha regarding honour. The mitzva to give precedence to and honour the kohen before the 'Israelite' applies when the kohen is more learned, or when the kohen and the 'Israelite' are equal in their spiritual level. But if the 'Israelite' is a greater Torah scholar than the kohen, there is no mitzva to give the kohen precedence over the Israelite. Moreover, the Sages said (Megilla 28a) that whoever gives precedence to a kohen who is an am ha'aretz over an Israelite who is a Torah scholar desecrates God and disgraces the Torah, and of him it is said (Mishlei 8:36): "All who hate me love death." And the Sages said in the Mishna (Horayot 3:8) that even a mamzer, whose lineage is blemished, if he is a Torah scholar, should be honoured more than a kohen gadol who is an am ha'aretz.

And so it is related in the Talmud (Yoma 71b): it happened that a certain kohen gadol came out of the Temple at the conclusion of Yom Kippur, and all the people accompanied him in an honourable procession to his home. When they saw Shemaya and Avtalyon, the two Sages of the generation, they left the kohen gadol and went with them. Afterwards, when Shemaya and Avtalyon came to greet the kohen gadol, he insulted them and said to them: "Let the descendants of the nations come in peace", intending to hint at their lowly lineage, for they were of a family of converts. Shemaya and Avtalyon answered him: better are the descendants of converts who conduct themselves in the way of Aharon than a son of Aharon who does not walk in the ways of Aharon the kohen, who was wise and pious.

As halakha, it is forbidden to give precedence to a kohen who is an am ha'aretz over an Israelite who is a Torah scholar. But when the kohen too is a Torah scholar, although by law the 'Israelite' who is wiser than he takes precedence, since both of them are Torah scholars and the kohen does not fall significantly below the level of the 'Israelite', the 'Israelite' may waive his honour in favour of the kohen, and this is a custom of piety, and he will merit length of days for it (Rema OḤ 167:14; MB 71). However, regarding an aliya to the Torah, in every case the kohen takes precedence, for the sake of peace (above 5:9).

sections.title_en: May One Make Use of a Kohen?
sections.body_en:
Since it is a mitzva to honour the kohen because he is designated for sacred roles, the halakha was decided (Yerushalmi, Berakhot 8:5) that one should not make use of a kohen, and one who makes use of him is like one who commits me'ila (shows disregard) with consecrated property. For Ezra the Scribe compared the vessels of the Temple and the kohanim to one another: just as one who uses the vessels of the Temple for mundane needs commits me'ila, so too one who makes use of the kohanim commits me'ila.

But there is a difficulty: it is the halakha that if a kohen stole and has no ability to pay, he must be sold as a Hebrew servant for a number of years, and with the payment for his servitude he returns what he stole.3 From this it follows that one may make use of a kohen. The answer to this is that because of the holiness of the kohen, one may not ask him for help and make use of him. But if the kohen on his own initiative wants to hire himself out for work, his employer may employ him in any work, since the kohen receives a wage for it and comes to the work of his own will. Likewise, if the kohen stole and has no ability to pay, since he is obligated to pay for what he stole, he may be sold as a Hebrew servant for a number of years.

According to this the halakha was decided that the prohibition of making use of a kohen applies only when one asks him for help in such a way that it would be unpleasant for him to refuse, for then it is as though one compels him to help. But if the kohen of his own accord wants to help, one may accept his help. Likewise, if one asks him for help in a way that he can refuse without feeling uncomfortable, if he agreed to help, one may accept his help. Indeed, some are stringent that as long as the kohen does not earn a wage or some other benefit, one should not make use of him (Taz OḤ 128:39). But according to most poskim, if the kohen is willing to help an Israelite, there is no prohibition in this (Rema OḤ 128:45; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 128:72).

A kohen whose daughter has left the community of Israel to marry among the gentiles – there is no longer a mitzva to sanctify him and honour him, because it is said (Vayikra 21:9): "And the daughter of any kohen, if she profanes herself by playing the harlot, she profanes her father." And although he himself is still obligated to raise his hands and keep all the mitzvot of the priesthood, the public is not obligated to honour him (see Rema OḤ 128:41).

notes_en.en: Slavery was permitted only in a period in which people died of hunger, and without slavery their existence would have been in danger. And then the Torah established mitzvot in order to protect the dignity and needs of the servant. But in a period in which a healthy society is able to provide food for the poor so that they do not die of hunger, it is obligated to abolish slavery from the world, as explained in Peninei Halakha, Shevi'it Ve-yovel 10:11.

sections.title_en: May a Kohen Work in a Hospital?
sections.body_en:
We have learned that a kohen may not become impure through the dead, that is, he may not touch a dead person or be with him under one roof. Therefore, according to many, a kohen may not study medicine, because both during his studies and during his work in a hospital he will be forced to become impure through the dead many times. And although there is a mitzva to save human life, since there are many Israelites who can study medicine, there is no need that specifically the kohanim, who may not become impure through the dead, should study medicine (Igrot Moshe YD 3:155).4

Regarding a kohen working in a hospital, the Aḥaronim disagree. Some forbid it, since there is a reasonable concern that a person will die there, and the kohen and the dead person will be found under one roof (Igrot Moshe there). And some are lenient and permit kohanim to work in a hospital, because each time they enter the hospital there is a doubt: perhaps at that time there is no dead person there, or the impurity will not pass from the area of the dead person to the place where the kohen works, such as where there are complete partitions between the wing of the dead person and the place where the kohen works; and likewise they join the opinion of those who hold that impurity passing from room to room through an opening is rabbinic, and for a great need they are lenient. But as for studying medicine, they agree that it is forbidden, because medical studies require the kohen to examine and touch dead bodies (Tzitz Eliezer 16:33; 17:8; Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach in Nishmat Avraham 370:2, note 2).

And Rav Goren ruled that ideally a kohen should not work in a hospital or study medicine, but if his soul is set on it, and the kohen's whole desire is only to study and practise medicine, one may permit him, because there is in it a mitzva of saving lives.5

In practice a kohen should not study medicine or work in a hospital, and if he very much wants to study medicine, or this is the only job offered to him, he should ask a Torah scholar.

notes_en.en: Responsa Maharam Schick OḤ 303; Melamed Le-ho'il 1:31; Aseh Lekha Rav 3:32; Yalkut Yosef 7, 30:7; Shevet Ha-levi 2:164. Likewise Rav Unterman recommended that kohanim not study medicine (as cited in his name in the book Torat Ha-kohen Ve-ha-levi, p. 85), and likewise Rav Herzog did not permit kohanim to study medicine; but because there are doubts in this, one cannot call an observant kohen who is a doctor a transgressor. And there are a few poskim who permitted it on account of saving lives or on account of the doubt about lineage; see the Encyclopedia of Halakha and Medicine, volume 3, entry Kohen.

The permission is based on the kohen wearing a chain with an ornament of a small spear made of metal that has touched a dead body, whose law of impurity is like that of avi avot ha-tum'a; and since according to many poskim there is no prohibition for the kohen to touch metal that touched a dead body, as brought in the Rambam, Hilkhot Evel 3:2, and in the Rema YD 369, it follows that he may wear the chain. And since he is already impure, there is no prohibition for him to become further impure through additional impurity as long as the metal touches his body (so he wrote in the Jubilee Volume for Rav Kirschenbaum, p. 29). And some disagreed and held that although he is impure from the chain, he may not become impure from actual impurity of the dead (Rav Bleich and Rav Halperin in the collections Halakha U-refu'a, volumes 3 and 4).

sections.title_en: Parents Blessing Their Children With Birkat Kohanim
sections.body_en:
It is said (Bamidbar 6:22-23): "And the Lord spoke to Moshe, saying: Speak to Aharon and to his sons, saying: Thus shall you bless the children of Israel…" From here it follows that only the kohanim may raise their hands and bless Israel, and an Israelite who recited Birkat Kohanim has transgressed this positive mitzva. The question is: how are Israelite parents accustomed to bless their children with Birkat Kohanim?

Some say that it is only with the raising of the hands that an Israelite may not bless, and therefore parents may bless their children with Birkat Kohanim, provided that they do not spread both their hands over the children in the manner of the kohanim (Baḥ); and on this basis some parents are accustomed to place only one hand on the head of the son or daughter while saying the verses.

And according to many, only when the 'Israelite' intends to recite Birkat Kohanim as its mitzva and halakha require does he transgress the mitzva. But when he says the blessing not at the time designated for it in the prayer, even if he spreads both his hands there is no prohibition in this, for it is clear that he does not intend the mitzva of Birkat Kohanim (MB 128:3 in the name of the Magen Gibborim, and Bei'ur Halakha there).
